back2basics.text: Priority Sector Lending is a policy tool used by the RBI to ensure that banks allocate a specified portion of their lending to sectors that are vital for the economy but often underserved by the financial system. PSL aims to promote inclusive growth by improving access to credit for these segments.

Banks, corporates, and financial institutions participate in this market to facilitate international trade, investment, and currency risk management. The Reserve Bank of India monitors this market to maintain currency stability and external sector health.

body.label: Ninth tranche of mineral block auctions
body.text: The Ministry launched the ninth tranche of e-auction for 20 critical and strategic mineral blocks under the Mineral (Auction) Rules.

body.label: Third tranche of exploration licence auctions
body.text: Alongside, the third tranche of auctions for Exploration Licences (EL) was launched, allowing private investment in exploration of 29 critical and deep-seated minerals.

body.label: Auction participation
body.text: Previously, 100 unique critical and strategic mineral blocks were offered in eight tranches, with 64 successfully auctioned, a success rate of 64%.

sections.heading: What did the Ministry of Mines launch in November 2026?

body.label: Minerals in critical blocks
body.text: The 20 blocks include minerals such as graphite, glauconite, vanadium, gallium, titanium, rare earth elements (REE), potash, halite, tungsten, phosphorite-limestone, bauxite, aluminous laterite, scandium, and rare metals.

body.label: States with auctioned blocks
body.text: Blocks are located in Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Rajasthan, Telangana, West Bengal, and Gujarat (for EL blocks).

body.label: Exploration licence blocks
body.text: The third tranche of EL auctions covers copper, potash, halite, vanadium, and rare earth elements among others in Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, West Bengal, Rajasthan, Telangana, and Gujarat.

sections.heading: Which minerals and states are involved in the auctions?

body.label: Reduced bidder requirement
body.text: The Mineral (Auction) Third Amendment Rules, 2026 reduced the minimum number of technically qualified bidders for the second round from three to two for Part D minerals, addressing a key reason for unsold blocks.

body.label: Automatic issuance of Letters of Intent
body.text: Letters of Intent will now be issued automatically through the Unified Mining Portal to streamline the process.

body.label: Auction formats
body.text: Critical mineral blocks are auctioned through a two-stage ascending forward auction where the highest revenue share wins, while exploration licence blocks use a two-stage descending reverse auction where the lowest revenue share wins.

body.label: Earlier reforms
body.text: These reforms build on earlier changes such as the Mineral (Auction) Second Amendment Rules, 2025 and Insurance Surety Bonds to improve ease of doing business and investor confidence.

sections.heading: What reforms were introduced to improve auction outcomes?

body.label: Strengthening mineral security
body.text: The auctions aim to secure domestic availability of critical and strategic minerals essential for sectors like clean energy, electric mobility, defence, aerospace, and electronics.

body.label: Encouraging private sector participation
body.text: Allowing private investment in exploration and mining promotes responsible mining and builds a resilient, self-reliant, and globally competitive mineral ecosystem.

body.label: Supporting energy transition
body.text: Access to critical minerals supports India's energy transition and industrial growth by ensuring supply for advanced manufacturing and strategic industries.

back2basics.text: Carbon markets are systems where carbon emission allowances or credits can be bought and sold, incentivizing reductions in greenhouse gas emissions. Emissions trading systems (ETS) set a cap on total emissions and allow entities to trade emission permits, promoting cost-effective mitigation. Voluntary markets operate without mandatory caps, enabling projects to generate carbon credits for sale. Measurement, reporting, and verification frameworks ensure transparency and accountability in emissions data.

2026-11-06-am-8ff7168e51.deck: At the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi, members reaffirmed their commitment to the BRICS Carbon Markets Partnership, focusing on capacity-building and experience-sharing without setting trading targets or timelines. body.label: Purpose
body.text: The Independent Drive Tests (IDTs) assess and verify real-time quality of mobile network services, including voice and data, provided by Telecom Service Providers (TSPs) to inform consumers and encourage service improvements.

body.label: Methodology
body.text: TRAI uses SIM cards from all TSPs over 2G, 3G, 4G, and 5G networks with multiple advanced test handsets to establish live data and voice sessions, monitored and analysed in real-time using advanced software systems.

body.label: Test Environments
body.text: Tests cover diverse usage environments such as city drives, hotspots, walk tests, public transport hubs, and highways to capture comprehensive network performance.

sections.heading: What is the purpose and methodology of TRAI's Independent Drive Tests?

body.label: Coverage Gap
body.text: Coverage gaps (samples with poor signal strength) varied among providers; for example, in Nuh district, Airtel had 346/15867 poor samples, BSNL 4021/15424, RJIL 784/15626, and VIL 327/15836.

body.label: Call Quality
body.text: Dropped calls were low for Airtel and VIL (0 in Nuh), while BSNL had 5 dropped calls out of 140; call silence instances over 3 seconds ranged from 5 to 35 among providers.

body.label: Data Speeds
body.text: Average download speeds in Nuh ranged from 6.78 Mbps (BSNL) to 130.28 Mbps (RJIL); upload speeds ranged from 6.21 Mbps (BSNL) to 14.26 Mbps (Airtel).

sections.heading: What were the key findings of the mobile network quality assessments in Nuh & Palwal?

body.text: Airtel, RJIL, and VIL showed zero coverage gaps in Mumbai, while MTNL had 13057 poor samples out of 3687, indicating data inconsistency or reporting issue.

body.label: Call Quality
body.text: Dropped calls were minimal, with Airtel having 1/510 and VIL 0/509; call silence instances were low, with 2 for Airtel and 1 for VIL.

body.label: Data Speeds
body.text: Average download speeds were 133.86 Mbps for Airtel, 248.93 Mbps for RJIL, and 89.04 Mbps for VIL; MTNL recorded 0 Mbps download and upload speeds.

sections.heading: How did mobile network quality vary in Mumbai LSA according to TRAI's report?

body.label: Coverage Gap
body.text: Coverage gaps were significant; for city drives, Airtel had 8393/37595 poor samples, BSNL 13481/31483, RJIL 10750/37912, and VIL 13557/22487.

body.label: Call Quality
body.text: Dropped calls in city areas ranged from 1 (RJIL) to 17 (VIL) out of total calls; on highways, dropped calls were also notable, e.g., 15/50 for BSNL.

body.label: Data Speeds
body.text: Average city download speeds ranged from 2.27 Mbps (BSNL) to 103.49 Mbps (RJIL); highway speeds were slightly lower but comparable.

back2basics.text: The Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA) is a law aimed at preventing money laundering and confiscating property derived from or involved in money laundering. The Enforcement Directorate (ED) is the central agency responsible for investigating offenses under this Act. Money laundering involves disguising illegally obtained money as legitimate income, which impacts economic security and governance.

This case highlights the role of ED under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA) and the challenges in tackling financial crimes affecting economic security.

back2basics.text: A geosynchronous orbit is a circular orbit around Earth with an orbital period matching Earth's rotation period, allowing satellites to appear stationary relative to the surface. This orbit is ideal for communication and navigation satellites as they maintain a fixed position relative to the ground, enabling consistent coverage.

back2basics.text: Regulatory bodies like the Atomic Energy Regulatory Board oversee the safety and security of nuclear energy operations. They ensure that nuclear plants comply with strict safety standards to protect people and the environment. Such bodies balance enabling technological growth with enforcing safety norms, especially when new players enter the sector.

This assurance comes amid policy shifts opening the sector to private players, highlighting the regulator's dual role of enabling growth and enforcing strict safety norms.
